Science.summary: A huge 10-sided atmospheric pattern has appeared around Saturn’s south pole, giving the planet a surprising counterpart to its famous northern hexagon. Hubble data suggest the strange decagon only began emerging in the past few years and is still growing stronger. Researchers hope continued observations will reveal why it suddenly formed and whether it could persist for decades.

Science.title: Igniting Roman’s Journey
Science.summary: Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. The mission launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Aug. 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Roman pairs a large […]

Science.title: ‘Not-quite primordial’ black holes may explain baffling JWST discovery
Science.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope seems to have discovered more ancient black holes than theory had predicted, and now we have a new way to explain why

Science.title: Satellites spot forest stress two years before bark beetle die-offs become apparent
Science.summary: Satellite measurements detected declining photosynthetic activity in Western U.S. forests two years before bark beetle mortality appeared in aerial detection surveys, according to new University of Utah-led research.

Science.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
Science.summary: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.

Science.title: Antarctic expedition reveals why Southern Ocean clouds remain one of climate science's greatest challenges
Science.summary: The Southern Ocean plays a pivotal role in regulating Earth's climate, yet the clouds that blanket this remote region remain among the least understood features in atmospheric science. By controlling both incoming sunlight and outgoing heat, these clouds strongly influence Earth's energy balance.

Science.title: Soft nanoscale confinement prevents ice, exposing water's liquid-to-glass transition
Science.summary: An international collaboration of researchers has used ANSTO's facilities to uncover new properties of one of the most fundamental everyday materials, water, and answer an important scientific question. The findings, published in Nature Communications, have practical implications for understanding water at very low temperatures. The findings are relevant to cryopreservation of biological materials, food-freezing technologies and understanding water in living cells, where it is often confined at the nanoscale.

Science.title: 'Green thumb' molecule helps leaf stalks grow in crowded conditions
Science.summary: Potassium (K) is one of the three essential nutrients for plants. It plays a critical role in a wide range of processes, including cell growth, photosynthesis and regulation of water balance. Plants take up K from the soil and circulate it throughout their bodies via molecules called K+ channels. The function of one such K+ channel (called AKT5) in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana has remained a mystery, despite more than 30 years of study.

Science.title: From peas to potatoes, AI identifies nearly 800 promising plant proteins for food and cosmetics
Science.summary: Scientists from Leeds' School of Food Science and Nutrition have developed an advanced AI process that can rapidly identify plant proteins capable of acting as emulsifiers from tens of millions of initial candidates. To date, it has identified nearly 800. The discovery will cut years of costly trial-and-error research and bring the next generation of plant-based foods and cosmetics closer.

Science.title: Hot subdwarfs come into focus as AI scans thousands of stars in Gaia data
Science.summary: There are myriad ways of "being a star," and scientists spend years trying to uncover and understand them. One unusual type is the so-called hot subdwarf—small stars that burn mysteriously hot for their size. Scientists from the Faculty of Physics and the Faculty of Mathematics and Informatics at Vilnius University (VU) are working to explain this strange phenomenon and recently made important breakthroughs.

Science.title: Tiny fossils reveal big insights about ant ancestors
Science.summary: Two tiny ant fossils recovered in southern Saskatchewan are helping scientists better understand the evolutionary history of modern ants. Ant fossils dating from 72–56 million years ago are rare. What happened to insects such as ants during this period that saw a mass extinction wipe out all non-bird dinosaurs? How did that event reshape their world?

Science.title: Perseverance rover watches Earth vanish behind Martian moon
Science.summary: Earth and the Martian moon Phobos dance together in a series of images recently acquired by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover. Earth appears as a point of light in the Martian sky, disappearing behind the crescent of Phobos, the larger of Mars' two moons.

Science.title: China's private, reusable Pallas-1 rocket aces debut launch (video)
Science.summary: Galactic Energy's new Pallas-1 rocket aced its debut launch on Monday (Aug. 31), successfully reaching orbit. The vehicle's first stage did not attempt a landing, however.

Science.title: Immune therapy engineered inside the body eases multiple sclerosis
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02765-1 Results from a small trial suggest a modified virus can instruct the immune system to wipe out disease-causing cells.

Science.title: One immune switch may help drive aging across the body
Science.summary: Aging may be partly fueled by immune cells losing their ability to clear away damaged, inflammation-promoting cells. Blocking a single receptor restored that cleanup process in mice, reducing inflammation and helping their organs, muscles, and memory remain remarkably youthful.

Science.title: Ancient “living fossils” may reveal how complex life began
Science.summary: A newly discovered microbe living inside ancient stromatolite communities may offer a rare look at how complex life first emerged. Researchers captured the first direct images of an Asgard archaeon physically connected to a bacterium, with the two microbes appearing to exchange nutrients and other compounds. Scientists think similar partnerships billions of years ago may have helped produce the first complex cells.

Science.title: The Arctic melt season is a week longer now than it was in the 1980s, new research on sea ice trends shows
Science.summary: Relatively few people have been to the Arctic, and even fewer have set foot in Antarctica. Most people rely on imagination and the media to visualize these landscapes and the ways they are changing.

Science.title: NASA to Cover Progress 96 Spacecraft Launch, Docking
Science.summary: NASA will provide live coverage of the launch and docking of a Roscosmos cargo spacecraft carrying about three tons of food, fuel, and supplies for the crew aboard the International Space Station. Science.title: Early mammals weren't all loners—some may have lived in pairs alongside the dinosaurs
Science.summary: About 200 million years ago, furry, little egg-laying creatures evolved the ability to feed their offspring with a secretion from special glands: milk. Their evolutionary journey continued, and by about 160 million years ago, the first mammals with a real placenta had come into being. Instead of laying eggs, they gave birth to live young that had been connected directly to their mother via a placenta during pregnancy, allowing the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste products.

Science.title: Lavish private bath used by Roman emperor and 'high-status residents' discovered at imperial palace in Serbia
Science.summary: The ancient bath complex was tucked in a tower in the corner of the royal palace and reveals unique architecture.

Science.title: Hubble spots a mysterious 10-sided 'decagon' growing around Saturn's south pole
Science.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope spied a large atmospheric phenomenon on Saturn: a decagon surrounding the south pole.

Science.title: NASA’s Hubble Spies Superbubble Scene
Science.summary: This Hubble Space Telescope image features a sprawling cosmic vista called N44.

Science.title: Rocket issues delay 1st-ever private mission to Venus: 'We are awaiting Neutron readiness'
Science.summary: The first-ever private mission to Venus is still groundbound due to delays with its launch vehicle, Rocket Lab's Neutron. But team members remain bullish on the groundbreaking mission.

Science.title: India sends Earth-imaging satellite toward geosynchronous orbit in milestone launch (video)
Science.summary: India launched an Earth-imaging satellite toward geosynchronous orbit today (Sept. 3) —something it had not previously done successfully.

Science.title: 'The apple you eat isn't the apple your granddaughter will eat': What's on the menu in a warming world?
Science.summary: Almost every aspect of our food system will be transformed by climate change.

Science.title: Traces of nearly 4 million coins reveal how Rome achieved economic integration
Science.summary: For centuries, the study of ancient history relied primarily on interpreting classical texts and examining inscriptions and archaeological remains at their sites of origin or in museums. In recent years, however, a little-known transformation has profoundly changed this landscape. The digitization of extensive archaeological collections, coupled with the development of quantitative methods that can integrate millions of scattered records, is ushering in a new era of historical research. Like other scientific disciplines that have benefited from processing colossal amounts of information, archa

Science.title: Parliamentary motions show growing AI use, with no disclosure from MPs
Science.summary: The two research teams have developed and used AI detectors trained on thousands of political motions in Sweden and the UK. What surprised the researchers was not that politicians were using AI—but that not a single one disclosed this openly.

Science.title: New map of a male fly central nervous system includes all 166,000 neurons — and enables direct comparisons to female fly brain
Science.summary: A new map of the adult male fruit fly brain and nerve cord includes over 166,000 neurons and the millions of connections between them.

Science.title: Light-triggered interface lets adhesive peel cleanly and rebond through 15 cycles
Science.summary: Adhesives are essential in electronics, vehicles and other products, but they can hinder repair and recycling when bonded parts are difficult to separate cleanly. A research team led by The University of Osaka has developed a prototype light-responsive adhesive that can be selectively detached from an illuminated surface without leaving observable residue. The adhesive film can then be rebonded by heating and reused after a second ultraviolet wavelength helps reset its molecular interactions.

Science.title: 'Strange New Worlds'' latest episode is a soap opera spoof, but hasn't 'Star Trek' always been a soap opera in space?
Science.summary: The latest 'Strange New Worlds' takes the silliness to warp factor nine, but soap opera plots have long been part of the 'Star Trek' mix

Science.title: Predictive tools can confuse rare mutations with dangerous ones
Science.summary: When a patient's DNA is read, it is compared with a reference version of the human genome. This allows geneticists and rare disease experts to look at a list of places where the patient's DNA differs. Most variations will be harmless and shared with millions of other people, but some can cause illness.

Science.title: China reaches solar energy milestone — what does this mean for the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter?
Science.summary: China is rapidly expanding its ability to harness renewable energy sources.

Science.title: A molecular brake that keeps muscle architecture in check
Science.summary: Every movement we make, from blinking to sprinting, depends on the ability of muscle fibers to contract in a rapid and coordinated way. Achieving this precision requires an intricate internal membrane network known as the transverse tubule, or T-tubule, system. These narrow membrane invaginations carry electrical signals from the cell surface deep into the muscle fiber, where they trigger the release of calcium needed for contraction.

Science.title: Comet McNaught put on a surprise show this summer: Here's how to spot it before it fades
Science.summary: Comet McNaught brightened dramatically during two outbursts around perihelion as it made a close approach to the sun.

Science.title: Astronomers discover mysterious 10-sided cloud structure at Saturn's south pole
Science.summary: A mysterious giant 10-sided pattern of clouds has recently formed around Saturn's south pole, a new study finds.

Science.title: Nanoscale multiferroic materials open the path to efficient magnetic memory technology
Science.summary: With the rapid spread of cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data centers, global energy consumption is rising to new heights. A promising way to reduce this burden is to develop memory devices that store information magnetically yet are written using electric fields. Magnetic memories are nonvolatile, meaning stored information is retained without a power supply.

Science.title: Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
Science.summary: Scientists discovered that more than 500 species of vesper bats possess two separate sets of antibody genes, an immune arrangement never before found in mammals. The surprising system could help explain how bats tolerate so many viruses without becoming seriously ill.

Science.title: Psilocybin may protect against a common, debilitating side effect of chemotherapy, early study finds
Science.summary: A psychedelic best known for its effects on the brain may also protect peripheral nerves from chemotherapy damage, early research suggests.

Science.title: ADHD may have a surprising creative advantage
Science.summary: Some of the attention patterns that make ADHD challenging may also help spark creativity by allowing the brain to explore more ideas and unexpected connections. Researchers think creative activities could potentially channel this “defocused attention” while helping strengthen the brain systems involved in focus and self-control.

Science.title: Ig Nobel Prize winners reveal why babies smell better than teenagers
Science.summary: Babies smell wonderful—at least to their parents. An international research team of Ilona Croy, Tomasz Frackowiak, Thomas Hummel and Agnieszka Sorokowska investigated why teenagers lose this special olfactory advantage and has now been awarded an Ig Nobel Prize for the research.

Science.title: September brings a dazzling Venus and a glowing Harvest Moon
Science.summary: September’s sky features brilliant Venus, the Milky Way’s hazy center, and the seasonal turning point of the equinox. The month ends with a glowing Harvest Moon rising near Saturn and faint Neptune.

Science.title: NASA Revamps Challenge Linking Community College Studies to Aerospace Careers
Science.summary: Community college students across the U.S. now have another opportunity to discover how their education can lead to fulfilling roles at the forefront of aerospace, science, engineering, and technology. The updated NASA Community College Aerospace Scholars (NCAS) student challenge invites students to learn about the agency and its missions, engage with NASA experts, and explore […]

Science.title: An ancient 'supervolcano' has been found hiding beneath eastern England. But experts say there's not enough evidence to call it that.
Science.summary: Geologists recently identified a 454.4 million-year-old volcano on England's east coast, but whether the structure can be considered a "supervolcano" remains an open question.

Science.title: How El Nino is choking the Panama Canal
Science.summary: The Panama Canal will restrict the number of vessels transiting the crucial waterway from Friday for only the second time because of drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon.

Science.title: Iron helped scientists trace Earth's oxygen. Now it's telling a bigger story
Science.summary: For decades, scientists have studied iron preserved in ancient rocks to reconstruct how Earth's oceans and atmosphere became rich in oxygen. A new study suggests iron has recorded other major transformations too.

Science.title: 'Power of disorder' tames CF₄, a semiconductor greenhouse gas that can persist for 50,000 years
Science.summary: Among the gases used in semiconductor manufacturing, tetrafluoromethane (CF₄) is a greenhouse gas more than 6,000 times as potent as carbon dioxide.

Science.title: 'Empty nest' can trigger loneliness and loss in older parents, study finds
Science.summary: Older parents can experience loneliness, emotional distress and a loss of purpose when their children leave home, according to a new pilot study by the University of Hertfordshire.

Science.title: Scientists just overturned a century-old physics assumption
Science.summary: Scientists at Carnegie Mellon University have discovered an unexpected form of the Hall effect, overturning the long-held assumption that this electrical response only appears when a magnetic field points perpendicular to a material. Beyond expanding a century-old principle of physics, the finding could eventually lead to simpler magnetic sensors for electronics, transportation, and medical technologies.

Science.title: Nations expanding their research programmes impose sweeping penalties for malpractice
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02517-1 India, Peru and Vietnam are rolling out policies that limit opportunities for scientists who fall foul of research-integrity guidelines.

Science.title: Buried underpants and a new definition of kissing win 2026 Ig Nobel prizes
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02650-x The awards highlight weird, funny and improbable research that also makes you think.

Science.title: 'A new mission starting today': 8 years after launch, BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival
Science.summary: After nearly eight years traveling through the inner solar system, the trailblazing BepiColombo spacecraft has finally begun its arrival at Mercury.

Science.title: How a plant's refusal to self-pollinate could help India grow more of its own cooking oil
Science.summary: Most people assume plants reproduce through whatever pollen happens to land on them. This is not true. A collaborative research initiative involving the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IITGN) has mapped and functionally tested the genes that control a natural "self-rejection" system in two widely grown Indian oilseed crops, Brassica rapa (mustard) varieties toria and yellow sarson. This system governs the molecular "lock-and-key" mechanism in certain mustard plants that allows them to reject their own pollen.

Science.title: 'There is no conflict between quantum physics and gravity': Physicists prove Einstein's 'happiest thought' holds true at quantum scales
Science.summary: Physicists have proven a 100-year-old prediction of relativity by showing that Einstein's equivalence principle holds at quantum scales.

Science.title: How an unassuming wildflower thrives in salt-laden air that kills other plants
Science.summary: On the windswept coasts of Oregon and California lives an unassuming little plant that can withstand salty blasts that kill its inland counterparts. It's called the yellow monkeyflower. Now, researchers are beginning to understand how it manages to thrive in conditions that leave other plants burned, brown and withered.

Science.title: Built to last or break down: Ring size tunes biodegradable plastic lifetimes
Science.summary: Biodegradable plastics should be tough enough for use yet able to break down at an appropriate rate afterward. Researchers at the University of Osaka show that changing the size of rings threaded onto a biodegradable polymer can tune both its toughness and enzymatic degradation, offering a way to design material lifetimes. The study is published in ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.

Science.title: Peatland Fires Darken Skies in Indonesia
Science.summary: With Indonesia gripped by drought, fires are smoldering on the surface and underground.

Science.title: Rapid simulation of heat propagation through multiple rods
Science.summary: There is an elegant mathematical equation behind many different natural phenomena. From the fractal pattern of a romanesco cauliflower sitting on a grocery store shelf to the flow of rivers, they all have underlying mathematical properties. The way heat propagates from one object to another also has a strikingly complex mathematical basis.

Science.title: Magic-mushroom compound blocks a severe side effect of chemotherapy, in mice
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02744-6 Study shows that psilocybin acts on nerves to prevent the painful condition called peripheral neuropathy.

Science.title: This was always the way: 'The Mandalorian and Grogu' is finally on Disney+
Science.summary: This 'Star Wars' spin-off movie disappointed at the box office, but it could find renewed life as a streaming smash hit.

Science.title: Even second graders can reason like scientists—if we ask them the right way
Science.summary: When a child asks "Why does a blowfish puff up?" we often jump in with facts. But what if we paused and suggested that they ask instead, "How does a blowfish puff up?" It may seem like splitting hairs, but this small shift in phrasing could help reshape future generations' capacity for reasoning and critical thought in science and beyond.

Science.title: Microbes—dead or alive—can be early indicators of soil health under regenerative farming
Science.summary: Researchers have demonstrated a series of biological tests that could serve as "proxies" for measuring how different regenerative agriculture practices could improve soil carbon—years before it would be possible to measure the carbon directly. The technique offers new insights into how effective various regenerative practices are at improving soil health.

Science.title: Beyond the 'Great Divide': What we really know about political polarization
Science.summary: Americans are deeply divided. At least that's what we've been told for years. But how divided are we really? A new review suggests the answer may depend on how researchers ask the question.

Science.title: Warming seas could shrink most mollusks by 2100, but some may grow
Science.summary: Research led by scientists at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette challenges a long-held assumption about the effects of climate change on marine life: Warmer oceans won't simply make animals smaller.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11091-5 Ketone homologation via palladium-catalysed decarboxylative rearrangement
